abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel information-theoretic framework for analyzing speech recognition systems that fundamentally reconceptualizes the relationship between acoustic observations and linguistic priors. Traditional approaches rely on conditional probability formulations that treat acoustic and language modeling as separable components. We propose a unified entropy-based paradigm where speech recognition is reframed as a rate-distortion optimization problem across the speech communication channel. This perspective reveals that current end-to-end models implicitly implement an information bottleneck that may not align with optimal linguistic encoding strategies. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that the widely-adopted maximum likelihood training objective is equivalent to minimizing a variational upper bound on the true recognition entropy. Furthermore, we establish formal connections between attention mechanisms in neural architectures and variable-rate source coding principles. The framework provides new analytical tools for understanding model compression and reveals fundamental limits of current autoregressive decoding strategies. Experimental validation on benchmark datasets confirms theoretical predictions about model behavior under various encoding regimes. This paradigm shift opens new research directions for understanding why certain architectural choices outperform others and provides a principled approach to designing speech recognition systems with theoretical performance guarantees.

This paper presents a significantly enhanced theoretical analysis of deep neural network-based acoustic modeling by introducing a hierarchical latent variable formulation that addresses fundamental limitations in current hidden Markov model theory. Traditional hybrid DNN-HMM systems suffer from the conditional independence assumption that fails to capture temporal dependencies in speech dynamics. We develop a novel theoretical framework based on factor graphs that allows explicit modeling of long-range contextual dependencies while maintaining computational tractability. The proposed formulation extends the classical forward-backward algorithm to incorporate neural network-based state emission probabilities within a rigorous probabilistic graphical model. Our analysis proves that this approach achieves lower bounds on the true data likelihood compared to standard conditional training, particularly for contexts involving coarticulation and speaking rate variations. The theoretical results are supported by rigorous mathematical proofs establishing convergence properties and complexity bounds. Experimental evaluations on the Switchboard and LibriSpeech corpora demonstrate substantial word error rate reductions of 12-18% over state-of-the-art baselines. This work provides a principled theoretical foundation for designing acoustic models that better capture the stochastic nature of speech production while maintaining the interpretability advantages of classical speech recognition theory.

We introduce a groundbreaking modular architecture for spoken language understanding that departs from traditional pipeline designs by implementing a neuro-symbolic integration framework. Existing systems treat intent detection and slot filling as separate tasks or jointly optimize them without exploiting their inherent structural relationships. Our proposed paradigm implements a differentiable logical reasoning layer that explicitly encodes linguistic constraints between semantic components. The system consists of three novel modules: a pre-trained speech encoder that produces frame-level representations, a constraint-aware semantic parser that applies formal grammar rules through differentiable operations, and a feedback mechanism that enables top-down semantic influence on acoustic processing. This design enables the system to handle zero-shot generalization to new intents by composing learned semantic primitives according to formal logical rules. Extensive evaluation on the SLURP and SNIPS datasets demonstrates that our approach achieves unprecedented robustness to speech recognition errors and handles compositional intents that confound existing methods. The modular nature allows independent updating of components without full retraining. By bridging symbolic reasoning and neural learning, this work establishes a new design philosophy for spoken language understanding systems that combines the generalization advantages of symbolic AI with the pattern recognition capabilities of deep learning.

This paper presents a substantially improved multi-channel speech enhancement system designed for far-field conversational AI applications. Current beamforming approaches face significant challenges in dynamic acoustic environments with moving speakers and varying noise conditions. We propose a novel adaptive neural beamformer that combines delay-and-sum preprocessing with a attention-based post-filter that dynamically estimates spatial and spectral characteristics. The system incorporates a speaker tracking module based on geometric deep learning that maintains stable speaker representation even during movement. A key innovation is the proposed cross-channel attention mechanism that learns to weight frequency bands based on their reliability in specific spatial configurations. The training procedure utilizes a multi-task learning objective combining signal-level enhancement metrics with automatic speech recognition performance, ensuring the enhanced signals optimize end-to-end application quality rather than just signal distortion measures. We introduce a new loss function that balances preserving speech intelligibility with suppressing interfering sources. Evaluation on the CHiME-6 and VoxConverse datasets shows significant improvements in word error rate reduction and speaker diarization accuracy compared to prior art. The system operates in real-time with a latency under 50ms, making it suitable for production deployment in voice assistants and video conferencing systems.
